lesson.title: A Safety Net for Old Age: The Social Security Act of 1935
lesson.summary: Signed on August 14, 1935, the Social Security Act created a national system of old age insurance and unemployment benefits, permanently changing what Americans could expect from their federal government.
lesson.body:
The Depression exposed a hard truth: private savings, family support, and local charity simply could not protect most elderly and unemployed Americans from poverty once a crisis reached national scale. Millions of older workers who had counted on savings or family had watched both evaporate by the mid 1930s, and there was no federal system in place to catch them.

In 1934, Roosevelt created the Committee on Economic Security and put Secretary of Labor Frances Perkins, the first woman ever to serve in a presidential cabinet, in charge of drafting a comprehensive plan. The resulting bill passed Congress and Roosevelt signed the Social Security Act on August 14, 1935.

The law established old age insurance funded by a new payroll tax split between workers and employers, a federal unemployment insurance system administered jointly with the states, and aid programs for dependent children and the blind. It was designed as social insurance rather than charity: workers paid into the system and earned a claim on benefits later, which made it politically durable in a way relief programs were not.

The act had real limits from the start. Agricultural and domestic workers were excluded from old age insurance, a compromise Roosevelt needed to secure the votes of Southern Democrats in Congress, and one that disproportionately shut out Black workers and women in those jobs across the South.

The first monthly retirement check went out in January 1940 to Ida May Fuller of Vermont. Alongside the Wagner Act, passed the same year, the Social Security Act marked what historians call the Second New Deal, a shift from emergency relief toward permanent structural programs meant to outlast the Depression itself.
